paragraphs: The next aspect of the House of Representatives I shall take up is the appointment of its members among the individual States, which is to be determined by the same rule as direct taxes.

No one argues that the number of people in each State should not be the standard for fixing the share of those who are to represent that State's people. Using the same rule for the appointment of taxes will probably be disputed just as little, though the rule rests on a different principle in this case. For representation, the rule is understood to refer to the personal rights of the people, with which numbers have a natural and universal connection. For taxation, it refers to the proportion of wealth, of which numbers are in no case a precise measure and in ordinary cases a very poor one. But the rule is imperfect as applied to the relative wealth and contributions of the States, and yet it is plainly the least objectionable of the rules that could be put into practice. America had also given it general approval too recently for the Convention not to prefer it readily.

All this is admitted, it will perhaps be said. But does it follow, from admitting numbers as the measure of representation, or slaves added to free citizens as a ratio of taxation, that slaves ought to be counted in the numerical rule of representation? Slaves are regarded as property, not as persons. They ought therefore to be counted in estimates of taxation, which rest on property, and left out of representation, which is regulated by a census of persons. This is the objection as I understand it, stated in its full force. I shall be just as fair in stating the reasoning that may be offered on the opposite side.

"We accept the doctrine," one of our Southern brethren might say, "that representation relates more directly to persons, and taxation more directly to property, and we join in applying this distinction to the case of our slaves. But we must deny that slaves are regarded merely as property and in no respect whatever as persons. The true state of the case is that they share in both qualities: our laws treat them in some respects as persons and in others as property. The slave is forced to labor, not for himself, but for a master. He can be sold by one master to another. He can be restrained in his liberty and chastised in his body at any time by the whim of another. In these respects the slave may seem to be degraded from the human rank and classed with those irrational animals that the law calls property. On the other hand, he is protected in his life and limbs against the violence of everyone else, even the master of his labor and his liberty, and he is himself punishable for any violence he commits against others. In these respects the slave is just as plainly regarded by the law as a member of the society, not as part of the irrational creation; as a moral person, not as a mere article of property. The federal Constitution therefore decides very properly on the case of our slaves when it views them in the mixed character of persons and property. This is in fact their true character. It is the character that the laws under which they live give them; and no one will deny that these laws are the proper test. For it is only on the pretext that the laws have turned the negroes into subjects of property that anyone disputes their place in the count of numbers. And it is admitted that if the laws were to restore the rights that have been taken away, the negroes could no longer be refused an equal share of representation with the other inhabitants.

"The question may be put in another light. Everyone agrees that numbers are the best scale of wealth and taxation, as they are the only proper scale of representation. Would the Convention have been impartial or consistent if it had left the slaves off the list of inhabitants when the shares of representation were calculated, and put them on the lists when the tariff of contributions was fixed? Could anyone reasonably expect the Southern States to join in a system that counted their slaves as men to some degree when burdens were to be imposed, but refused to count them the same way when advantages were to be handed out? Might there not also be some surprise that those who reproach the Southern States for the barbarous policy of treating a part of their human brethren as property should themselves argue that the government of which all the States are to be parties ought to treat this unfortunate race more fully in the unnatural light of property than the very laws they complain of?

"Perhaps it will be answered that slaves are not counted in the estimate of representatives in any of the States that have them. They do not vote themselves, nor do they add to the votes of their masters. On what principle, then, ought they to enter into the federal estimate of representation? In rejecting them altogether, the Constitution would in this respect have followed the very laws that have been appealed to as the proper guide.

"A single observation answers this objection. It is a fundamental principle of the proposed Constitution that the total number of representatives allotted to the individual States is to be fixed by a federal rule based on the total number of inhabitants. In the same way, the right to choose the number allotted to each State is to be exercised by whatever part of the inhabitants the State itself designates. The qualifications on which the right of suffrage depends are perhaps the same in no two States, and in some States the difference is very material. In every State, a certain proportion of inhabitants are deprived of this right by the State's constitution, yet they will be counted in the census by which the federal Constitution apportions the representatives. Seen this way, the Southern States could throw the complaint back. They could insist that the principle the Convention laid down required no regard to any State's policy toward its own inhabitants. It would follow that the slaves, as inhabitants, should have been admitted into the census at their full number, like other inhabitants whom the policy of other States does not admit to all the rights of citizens. But those who would gain from it give up insisting on this principle in all its rigor. All they ask is that the other side show equal moderation. Let the case of the slaves be treated as what it truly is, a peculiar one. Let both sides accept the compromising expedient of the Constitution, which regards the slaves as inhabitants, but as debased by servitude below the equal level of free inhabitants; which regards the SLAVE as stripped of two fifths of the MAN.

"After all, may we not take another ground on which this article of the Constitution can be defended still more easily? So far we have assumed that representation concerned persons only and not property at all. But is that assumption just? Government is instituted no less to protect the property of individuals than their persons. Property as well as persons, then, may be considered as represented by those who are charged with the government. On this principle, in several of the States, and particularly in the State of New York, one branch of the government is meant to be especially the guardian of property, and is elected accordingly by the part of the society most interested in that object of government. This policy does not prevail in the federal Constitution. The rights of property are placed in the same hands as the personal rights. Some attention ought therefore to be paid to property in choosing those hands.

"There is another reason why the votes the people of each State are allowed in the federal legislature ought to bear some proportion to the comparative wealth of the States. States do not, like individuals, have an influence over each other that comes from superior advantages of fortune. If the law gives a wealthy citizen only a single vote in choosing his representative, the respect and standing he gets from his fortunate situation very often steer the votes of others toward the objects of his choice. Through this imperceptible channel the rights of property are carried into the public representation. A State has no such influence over other States. It is not likely that the richest State in the Confederacy will ever sway the choice of a single representative in any other State. Nor will the representatives of the larger and richer States have any advantage in the federal legislature over the representatives of other States except what comes from their greater number alone. To whatever extent their greater wealth and weight may justly entitle them to an advantage, therefore, it ought to be secured to them by a larger share of representation. In this respect the new Constitution differs materially from the existing Confederation, and from that of the United Netherlands and other similar confederacies. In each of those, the effectiveness of the federal resolutions depends on the later and voluntary resolutions of the states that make up the union. Hence the states, though they hold an equal vote in the public councils, have an unequal influence, matching the unequal importance of these later and voluntary resolutions. Under the proposed Constitution, the federal acts will take effect without the individual States having to step in. They will depend merely on a majority of votes in the federal legislature. Consequently each vote will have equal weight and effect, whether it comes from a larger or smaller State, or from a State more or less wealthy or powerful. It will be just as with the votes individually cast in a State legislature by the representatives of unequal counties or other districts, which each have precisely equal value and effect. Or if there is any difference in the case, it comes from the difference in the personal character of the individual representative, rather than from any regard to the size of the district he comes from."

Such is the reasoning that an advocate for the Southern interests might use on this subject. It may seem a little strained at some points, yet on the whole I must confess that it fully reconciles me to the scale of representation the Convention has established.

In one respect, setting up a common measure for representation and taxation will have a very beneficial effect. The accuracy of the census Congress is to take will necessarily depend a good deal on the disposition, if not the co-operation, of the States. It is therefore very important that the States feel as little bias as possible toward inflating or shrinking their numbers. If the rule governed only their share of representation, they would have an interest in exaggerating their inhabitants. If it decided only their share of taxation, the opposite temptation would win out. By extending the rule to both objects, the States will have opposite interests that control and balance each other and produce the necessary impartiality.
